work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: In postremum iudicium (vel De fine ieiunii)

paragraphs.text: By the grace of God we have completed the first and middle contests of the most holy fast, and each of us, as far as he could, has gathered flowers from the meadow of virtue. Today the final peak of the contests has arrived. It sets harder labours before us, but it also weaves bright crowns, because the ends of every contest and of every virtue are glorious. That is why the perfect carry virtue through to the end. So let blessed David speak to this God-loving people the title found in the divine Scriptures: "To the end: do not destroy." Blessed David set this preface at the head of many of his psalms: "To the end: do not destroy." In other words, what you began well, bring to a good end.

The final peak of the contests sets glorious contests before us. They are not broken off by toil; they are carried through by longing. Toil on its own wastes the flesh and does the soul no good, but longing gives the soul wings and makes the body lighter. That is why we fast, brothers. We do not fast to wither the flesh. We fast to give the soul leisure, so that we may draw it away from human things and teach it to contemplate divine things. That is why we fast: to take up the bridle of self-control and to beat back the urges of desire, like the bucking of an unruly colt. That is why we fast: to cut away what our good teacher spoke of earlier, I mean many-headed vice, the dragon that has many heads.

The dragon's many heads are the many forms of vice. The first of its vices that he named was pride, for "the beginning of pride is to depart from the Lord." Nothing is more loathsome than pride. It is so great an evil that even the proud hate it. What proud man can bear to look on another proud man with a gentle eye? Is he not disgusted to see in another what he is not ashamed to have himself? That is how vice works. A man does not refuse the deed itself. The fornicator is ashamed to be called a fornicator, and the thing he enjoys doing he is ashamed to hear named. The proud man hates his own passion and loathes its name. That is why the prophet Isaiah, though he looks at every sin, aims the coming of God especially against the proud: "Behold, the day of the Lord of hosts is coming upon everyone who is insolent and proud and lofty." Then see what he does as he compares pride to various kinds of height. He calls the proud mountains and hills and cedars, and further on, walls and towers. Once he has shown how high they are, he describes how they will be pulled down. To see that Scripture attacks pride under so many names, listen to the prophet: "Behold, the day of the Lord of hosts is coming upon everyone who is insolent and proud, and upon every cedar of Lebanon, the high and lofty ones, and upon every oak of Bashan, and upon every high mountain, and upon every ship, and upon every sight of ships." He listed cedars, trees of Bashan, mountains, hills, walls and towers. Then, to show that he was not talking about things we see with our eyes but was attacking pride among human beings, he added: "And the height of men shall be brought low, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day." Look: "And the height of men shall be brought low, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day." He called pride a mountain, a hill, a wall and a tower. He did not mean a secure one, but one that only looks lofty.

If we chose to look closely, we would find that Scripture has also given these names to virtue among human beings. It called the virtue of a righteous man a wall and a tower, as when God says to Jeremiah: "Behold, I make you like an iron pillar and a bronze wall, and they will fight against you, but they shall not prevail." A wall fortified by godliness is one thing, and a wall raised up by pride is another. The one has only the look of a wall, while the other shines with real strength. Do not let this point slip past your soul, which loves to listen and to learn. Scripture often uses the same images for virtue and for vice. It does not confuse the nature of things, but it takes from an image what fits the bad sense and assigns to virtue what belongs to it. Divine Scripture called the proud man a cedar of Lebanon: "I saw the ungodly man exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was no more; I sought him, and his place was not found." But see, the righteous man is a cedar as well: "The righteous man shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall be multiplied like the cedar in Lebanon." It says "multiplied," not "lifted up." The righteous were called mountains, not because of the height of pride but because of the greatness of their virtue: "His foundations are on the holy mountains." What mountains are these, on which the foundations were laid? Listen to Paul: "You are God's building, built upon them." Those are mountains, but they are mountains of light. Notice, though, that the mountains of ungodliness are dark. The prophet speaks of them: "Woe to those who stumble on the dark mountains." By dark mountains he means the error of the demons and the elation of pride. By mountains of light he means the apostles, through whom God flashed forth. Usually the sun's rays reach the mountain peaks first, and in the same way God's kindness, as it rises, first reaches the heights of virtue. So Scripture calls the righteous mountains. Mountains take their nature from the earth yet rise above the earth, and in the same way the prophets and the righteous take their nature from human beings yet live a life beyond the human. Blessed David spoke of these mountains: "You shine forth wondrously from the everlasting mountains." For the light of godliness shone out through the prophets.

But let us return to our subject. How does Isaiah denounce pride? "And the height of men shall be brought low, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day." Here again, see how great is the teaching about the divinity of Christ. A prophet never speaks without breathing Christ, and he says nothing apart from Christ. He sings Christ's praises and declares the divinity of Christ's Father. If he mentions the Father, he makes the Son shine out in what he teaches about God. If he proclaims the Son, the Father flashes out first. If he speaks of the Father, he proclaims the Spirit. The Trinity cannot be separated, and its kingship cannot be divided.

What, then, does he say? "And the height of men shall be brought low, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day." For the eyes of the Lord are lofty, but man is lowly, "and the height of men shall be brought low." "And then they shall hide the idols their hands have made, carrying them into the caves and the holes of the earth and the clefts of the rocks, from the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his might, when he rises to shatter the earth." What fear of the Lord is he describing? Which Lord are they fleeing when they hide their idols? These things need no interpretation, because the words themselves bear witness: "And they shall hide the idols their hands have made, carrying them into the caves and the holes of the earth and the clefts of the rocks, from the face of the fear of the Lord, when he rises to shatter the earth"—that is, to judge the earth. And who is the judge? "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgement to the Son." Blessed David agrees with this when he says: "O God, give your judgement to the king."

But we need testimony that cannot be disputed or called forced if we are to answer those who object. So I must present testimony that is strong and clear enough to show that Isaiah's prophecy refers to Christ. Take the words "As I live, says the Lord, to me every knee shall bow and every tongue." Paul came forward and showed that this prophecy was taken up and applied to Christ, when he said: "Why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? For it is written: As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me." Paul's teaching removed the doubt of those who objected. In the same way, let the same witness come forward today and show who this Lord is, before whose fearful face and the greatness of whose might men will hide their idols.

Pay close attention, and go over the words again: "They shall hide the idols their hands have made, which their fingers fashioned, and they shall hide them in the caves and the holes of the earth and the clefts of the rocks, from the face of the fear of the Lord, when he rises to shatter the earth." Now blessed Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, says: "We give thanks to God, brothers, for all our affliction and for the persecutions you are enduring. This is evidence of the righteous judgement of God, so that you may be counted worthy of his kingdom, for which you are also suffering. For it is just in God's sight to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to give relief, along with us, to you who are afflicted, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. He will come from heaven with the angels of his power in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of his Son. They will pay the penalty of eternal destruction from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his might, when he comes to be glorified in his saints." Paul used the same words and brought forward the same prophecy. In this way he gives us eyes to look on the beauty of this teaching about God, and to recognize the one whom the prophets proclaimed and the Gospels praise. For it is one and the same God who arranged the former things well and clearly shaped the new. The tongue that spoke beforehand sang that he came down from above for our sake and lived among us in a form like ours. In doing so he did not dishonour his dignity before the ages but gave honour to his plan of salvation in the flesh. See the beauty of his teaching about God. Already I can see the gleaming of the cross too, and how it shows its flowers. They are flowers that do not wither, and they make a crown of righteousness.

The grace of the cross always shines. Time does not limit it, feasts do not divide it, and no festival confines it. Yet this commemoration has more to say on the subject. This cross became the sword that slew the dragon we mentioned a little while ago, of which Isaiah said: "And the Lord God will bring the holy sword, the great and strong one, upon the serpent, the ancient dragon." "And the Lord will bring his holy sword, the great and strong one." What is the great sword? What is the strong one? The Holy Spirit. The Lord will bring his holy sword upon the dragon and will slay the dragon. For the demons were destroyed through the Holy Spirit, as he himself says: "But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God..." Do you see the sword cutting? Listen also to Paul's interpretation: "Put on the breastplate of righteousness, and take the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God." The sword of the Spirit cuts away the dominion of the demons. It cut off the heads of the dragon, and it muzzles the wickedness of heretics. Let them respect the dignity of the Spirit. Let them fear the sovereignty of the holy and worshipful Spirit.

Let them consider how many people are being made divine today through the Holy Spirit, for it is from the Holy Spirit that they receive the form of deification. Is the one who shapes others into divinity himself a stranger to divinity? Do you not know the Spirit's power? Do you not know his working? Listen to Paul. He sets out clearly and plainly the unity, or rather the identity, of nature between the Spirit and God. He often called him the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ, so the heretics might take "Spirit" to mean not identity of nature but only that he belongs to God. A man is called a man of God because he came into being from God. In the same way, they might say, he is called the Spirit of God because God gave him, since he has his existence from God. So see how carefully Paul secures the point: "For God has revealed it to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. For just as no one knows what is in a man except the man's spirit that is in him, so also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit that is from God." If the Spirit were foreign to God's essence, how could he know it? Pay attention to how the words follow one another: "Just as no one knows the things of a man except the man's spirit that is in him, so also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God." And to secure the point again, he adds: "We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is from God." But see, my beloved, the counter-argument. Wickedness raises an objection. It says: "These very words show that the Spirit stands far below divine dignity, because he searches the depths of God." Yet the apostle added a complete answer to the question: "So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God." So he does not search as one who does not know. If the word offends you, and "searches" seems to you to imply that the Spirit lacks knowledge, what will you do when you see God searching too? If the word "search" troubles your mind, then when you see the God whom you yourself confess searching, will you suppose that he suffers from ignorance? Listen to Paul: "And the Spirit himself intercedes for us." Is this not about the Holy Spirit? It has often been said that Scripture calls the heart "spirit." For example: "A broken spirit is a sacrifice to God; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise." Besides, Paul himself explains that here he calls the heart "spirit": "The Spirit himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words; and he who searches the hearts"—whose hearts? Those of human beings—"searches the depths of God." God too often uses human words about himself, words that fall short of the divine meaning. They must be understood by their sense, not measured by their wording. God once said about the Jews: "If they hide on the top of Carmel, I will search them out from there and take them."

But see what they say. They have invented a strange title for the Spirit, and as if it were theirs to decide whether to honour him or not, they say: "We do not call the Spirit God, but a sanctifying power." Pay close attention, I beg you. "We do not call the Spirit God," they say, "but a sanctifying power." Is it a power able to sanctify by itself, or does it receive that power from another and pass it on? What exactly is this "sanctifying power"? Does it sanctify by its own authority and power, or does it borrow the power from God and hand it on? If it sanctifies by its own power, it is God. If it receives power from God and passes it on, it is no different from us. We too sanctify the baptized. By nature we are human beings, by God's grace, but in rank we are priests, appointed by God. No one can receive sanctification without a priest's hands. Then call the priest a sanctifying power too! But he is not a sanctifying power. He is a servant of the sanctifying power. So what do you take this name "sanctifying power" to mean? The Spirit? Is the Father not a sanctifying power, then? Do you dare to say that the Father is not a sanctifying power? Do you dare to say that the Son is not a sanctifying power? But if the Father sanctifies, the Son sanctifies and the Holy Spirit sanctifies, why do you not call each of them a sanctifying power?

But he uses respectful-sounding words to dress up his wickedness. I will make one brief argument and then move on. I would like to know why someone who thinks the Holy Spirit is foreign to the Godhead accepts the Holy Spirit in baptism. They say: "Mortal nature could not reach the Father first, so it first receives the Spirit's guidance. First," he says, "a person's soul is enlightened by the Holy Spirit. Then he advances to knowledge of the Son, and from the Son he advances to the Father."

See what strange steps their wickedness has invented! Both the Lord's own words and the actual practice fight against them. If things were as they say, I ought to be baptized not first into the name of the Father. I should first be made worthy of the lesser, then baptized into the Son to reach the middle, and then go on from the Son to meet the perfect. But in fact I am baptized first into the name of the Father. Why? The Saviour said: "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son."
Why also of the Son? Have you judged the Father's power to be inadequate, so that you bring in another power? Is the Father not able by himself to sanctify?

Either grant that the Trinity has one power and one Godhead, and then baptism has grace; or, if the nature is cut apart, you insult the Godhead. After a king's signature, will you add the signature of a slave? After the Master's authority, will you bring in the lowliness of creation? What does the Holy Spirit share with the Father? The power to set free? If the Spirit is a slave, how does he set free? He himself would owe thanks, if he has not been granted freedom. But to refute this blasphemy, let Paul speak here: "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." But we must also wait for the teaching of the Holy Spirit, so that the preaching of godliness may truly be sealed with the Holy Trinity. So let us end our sermon here. Let us secure our minds and wall ourselves in with the orthodox faith. Let us follow in the footsteps of the prophets and stay within the ramparts of the apostles, so that the arrows of wickedness can find no way in. The Lord Jesus will destroy them. To him be glory and power, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
